Background

Community science is a growing area where people who are not traditionally considered scientists assist with research projects. This can include providing data, assisting with project implementation, and analyzing data (Gosnell 2023). Community scientists can expand data collection efforts beyond what a single lab can accomplish and greatly enrich projects.

A recent example focused on using social media posts to determine the distribution of ornate spotted rays (Aetomylaeus vespertilio) (Araujo et al. 2020).

1

Previous research indicated eagle rays are nocturnal feeders, with 80% of their feeding activity occurring at night. The collected images included 76 shots of rays feeding, with 50 of those shot in daylight hours. Does this match expectations?

Make sure you include (6 points)

  • null hypothesis (1 point)

    • The proportion of eagle ray feeding activity during daylight is 20%.

  • alternative hypothesis (1 point)

    • The proportion of eagle ray feeding activity during daylight is not 20%.

  • explanation for test you will use (1.5 point)

  • I have two outcomes that I am comparing to a set proportion of success, so I will use a binomal test.

  • results from statistical test (1 point)

binom.test(50, 76, p = 0.20, alternative = "two.sided") 

    Exact binomial test

data:  50 and 76
number of successes = 50, number of trials = 76, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true probability of success is not equal to 0.2
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.5401240 0.7629432
sample estimates:
probability of success 
             0.6578947

or

binom.test(76-50, 76, p = 0.80, alternative = "two.sided") 

    Exact binomial test

data:  76 - 50 and 76
number of successes = 26, number of trials = 76, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true probability of success is not equal to 0.8
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.2370568 0.4598760
sample estimates:
probability of success 
             0.3421053
  • clear explanation of how results relate to your stated hypotheses (1.5 point)
    • since p<.001(<.05), I reject my null hypothesis. There is evidence that the proportion of rays feeding during the day is not 20%.

2

Scientists used imaging tools to gather extra information from the the images. Note different images provided different pieces of data due to the perspective. For example, they were able to use some pictures to determine both sex (male, female, unknown) and wing width for each individual. Data is available at

ray_data <- read.csv("ray_data.csv", stringsAsFactors = T)

Use the data to determine if wing width differs among sexes. Make sure you include (6 points)

  • null hypothesis (1 point)

  • H0: Wing width does not differ among sexes (i.e., \(\mu_{male}=\mu_{female}=\mu_{unknown}\))

  • alternative hypothesis (1 point)

  • HA: Wing width does differ among sexes (i.e., at least one \(\mu_\text{one measured group}\neq\mu_\text{other measured group}\))

  • explanation for test you will use (1.5 point)

  • I will use an ANOVA, a type of linear model, since I am comparing means among groups

  • results from statistical test (1 point)

width_model <- lm(width_cm~sex, ray_data)
plot(width_model)

Assumptions look ok, so I can check results.

library(car)

There is a significant difference among groups (F2,130=11,685, p<.001), so I reject the null that all groups are the same. To find which group is different, I can carry out post-hoc tests using the Tukey method to control for family-wise error rate.

The results indicate all groups have different average wing widths (all p<.001 for post hoc tests).

4

The dataset also gave a chance to consider how social the rays are. Scientists considered images of each sex to determine if they were photographed alone or in groups.

Male Female Unknown
Alone 38 6 14
In a group 4 22 49

Use the data to determine if sociality differs among sexes. Make sure you include (6 points)

  • null hypothesis (1 point)
  • H0: Ray sociality does not differ by sex
  • alternative hypothesis (1 point)
  • H0: Ray sociality does differ by sex
  • explanation for test you will use (1.5 point)
  • results from statistical test (1 point)
  • I will attempt to use a \(\chi^2\) test to compare proportions among the groups.
ray_ratio_table <- matrix(c(38, 6, 14, 4,22,49), 2,3, byrow = T)
colnames(ray_ratio_table) <- c("male", "female", "unknown")
rownames(ray_ratio_table) <- c("alone", "group")
chisq.test(ray_ratio_table)

    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  ray_ratio_table
X-squared = 54.834, df = 2, p-value = 1.239e-12

Test assumptions appear to be met (no warnings). The p-value is <. 05 (\(\chi^2_2\)=54.834, p<.001, so I reject the null hypothesis. I carry out post-hoc tests to see which groups are different than others.I will use the Holm’s methods to adjust for FWER.

library(rcompanion)
holm_correct <- pairwiseNominalIndependence(ray_ratio_table, compare="col", method = "holm")
library(rmarkdown)
Warning: package 'rmarkdown' was built under R version 4.4.3
paged_table(holm_correct[order(holm_correct$p.adj.Chisq), c("Comparison", "p.adj.Chisq")])

  • clear explanation of how results relate to your stated hypotheses (1.5 point)

  • results indicate that males are diffent than the other groups (all p<.05). ## 5

Ornate eagle rays have very long tails - they can be up to 2-3 m long. A few images were found that allowed both the tail and the wing width to be measured. Is there any relationship among these body parts? Data is available at

wing_tail_data <- read.csv("wing_tail_data.csv", stringsAsFactors = T)

Make sure you include (6 points)

  • null hypothesis (1 point)

  • H0: There is no relationship between tail length and wing width (\(\beta=0\))

  • alternative hypothesis (1 point)

  • H0: There is no relationship between tail length and wing width (\(\beta\neq0\))

  • explanation for test you will use (1.5 point)

  • I will use linear regression to compare the relationship between two continuous variables. I could also use/call this correlation and investigate correlation if I preferred.

  • results from statistical test (1 point)

plot(lm(tail_length_cm~wing_width_cm, wing_tail_data))

Assumptions appear to be met.

6

In general, do you see any issues with using this data or the analysis you completed? Please note at least potential concerns or issues with any of the above datasets or analysis.

Issues include these being from uncontrolled photos, so maybe more at day than night, in touristy areas, or of extreme (large,small, colorful) rays.

References

Araujo, Gonzalo, Christine Legaspi, Kinsey Matthews, Alessandro Ponzo, Andrew Chin, and B. Mabel Manjaji-Matsumoto. 2020. “Citizen science sheds light on the cryptic ornate eagle ray Aetomylaeus vespertilio.” Aquatic Conservation 30 (10): 2012–18. https://doi.org/10.1002/aqc.3457.
Gosnell, J Stephen. 2023. “What Is Community Science, and How Do I Get Involved?” Lessons in Conservation 13: 38–43.
